title: Wind Tunnel for Agent Markets and Pricing Collusion
one_liner: Simulate your pricing or buying agent against thousands of rival agents to see whether it drifts into tacit collusion, manipulation or first-offer traps before regulators or rivals do.
customer: Revenue-management and pricing-software vendors (hotels, multifamily, retail, insurance), marketplaces running agent-facing APIs, and the antitrust and compliance counsel who advise them. Regulators are a later customer.
problem: Academic work shows LLM pricing agents can converge on supracompetitive prices without communicating. Microsoft's Magentic Marketplace found agent buyers show strong first-proposal bias (a 10-30x advantage for response speed) and can be manipulated. Algorithmic pricing is already drawing antitrust suits and state laws, and nobody has a standard way to show a deployed pricing agent behaves competitively.
solution: Adapt the open-source Magentic Marketplace environment into a test harness with calibrated rival populations (LLM and RL agents). Run repeated-game tests measuring markups against a competitive baseline, information-leakage tests, and manipulation and first-offer sensitivity. Deliver an algorithmic pricing conduct report plus guardrails (randomization, no shared non-public data, price-parity limits) and re-test when the underlying model changes.
why_now: Agentic repricing is spreading, algorithmic-pricing enforcement is active, the simulation environment was open-sourced in late 2025, and models change every quarter so one-off audits go stale.
revenue_model: $40-$150k per audit, $5-$15k/month re-test subscriptions, and law-firm seat licenses.
non_obvious_insight: You cannot inspect intent inside a model, but you can test behavior in a sandbox economy. Like crash tests for cars, a standardized, reproducible test gives defendants a documented duty-of-care defense and gives regulators a common yardstick.
first_30_days: Adapt Magentic Marketplace to a hospitality-pricing scenario and write a methodology note. Approach 3 antitrust boutiques and 3 revenue-management vendors, and sell a $25k pilot audit.

title: Identical Object Kits for Robot Data Farms
one_liner: Manufacture and ship standardized kits of hundreds of everyday-object variants, panels of handles, hinges and knobs, and task fixtures, so that every home and lab collecting robot training data uses the same physical objects.
customer: Robot-learning startups and university labs, and the data-collection vendors that run gig-worker networks who record household demonstrations for humanoid and manipulation models.
problem: At-home robot data collection is booming, but contributors use whatever cups, jars and cabinet handles they own. That makes data hard to compare, hard to control for variation and impossible to replicate across sites. A robot learning to open a drawer needs the same drawer types in 500 places.
solution: A 'Kitchen-100' kit: 100 standardized, individually scanned objects (cups, lids, jars, tongs, utensils, packages), plus modular handle, hinge, latch and knob panels and drawer or door fixtures with known mass, friction and geometry. Ship to thousands of contributors and to labs. Sell new object sets monthly so datasets keep growing coherently, and bundle the digital twins (scans and physics parameters) for simulation.
why_now: Humanoid and robot-foundation-model companies are competing for training data in 2026, and coverage such as MIT Technology Review's April 2026 report on gig workers training humanoids at home shows the supply chain for that data is still improvised. Only a handful of vendors can collect at scale, and none owns the standardized physical layer.
revenue_model: Kit sales ($150 to $600 each in batches of hundreds or thousands), monthly new-object subscriptions, custom fixture builds for labs ($5k to $50k) and licensing of scan and physics data.
non_obvious_insight: The bottleneck for physical AI is not only more demonstrations but controlled, comparable ones. Whoever ships the same 100 objects to 5,000 kitchens gets a natural experiment in robot learning, and the kit sets the de facto benchmark. Old benchmarks (like a single reference set of household objects) are small and dated, so a manufacturing-scale, refreshable standard can become infrastructure.
first_30_days: Design and print or source a v0 kit of 50 to 100 objects and a set of handle panels. Scan each object and publish a free open dataset as marketing. Pitch 15 labs and 5 data-collection vendors with a pilot offer: 20 kits at cost plus a custom object of their choice. Target one vendor pilot of 200 kits.

title: Ratepayer Impact Statements for Data Centers
one_liner: An independent, quantified 'who pays' filing for every proposed data center, like an environmental impact statement but for your electric bill.
customer: Data center developers who need a credible neutral document to win zoning or PUC approval ($50-150k per project). County governments, state consumer advocates and ratepayer coalitions ($15-40k per docket) also buy it.
problem: 7 in 10 Americans oppose data centers in their community and New York imposed a hyperscale moratorium. Residential rates are up 7.3% and utilities requested a record $31B in hikes in 2025. Nobody can credibly say how much of a specific rate case or interconnection cost a given project causes, so each side hires ad hoc experts and the fight runs on vibes.
solution: An open, auditable cost-causation model built on FERC Form 1, EIA-861, large-load tariff filings, IRP capacity plans and PJM auction results. It outputs a 10-year per-household bill delta for a specific project under different tariff terms (minimum take, collateral, bring-your-own-capacity). Deliverables are a standardized Ratepayer Impact Statement and a witness-ready exhibit. A free state-by-state 'who pays' scorecard is the top of the funnel.
why_now: Affordability is a midterm issue and opposition is now bill-driven. Utilities are adopting large-load tariffs whose terms can be modeled. Capacity prices at the cap make cost shifts visible in dollars per MWh.
revenue_model: Per-project fee from developers, per-docket fee from advocates and counties, and an annual subscription for PUC staff. Independence comes from a published fee schedule and a methodology committed in advance, as with credit rating agencies.
non_obvious_insight: Insiders dismiss opposition as NIMBY, but it is really about bills, and bills are quantifiable. Whoever owns the accepted number owns the approval process. Both sides will pay for it, the way both sides accept an appraisal.
first_30_days: Publish a free 'Who Pays' report for three states using public filings. Email 10 state consumer advocate offices and 20 county planning departments. Offer a $12k pilot impact statement on one live docket. Approach two mid-size developers who are stuck in a zoning fight.

title: Orphan Fleet Depot for Bankrupt-Maker Electric Buses
one_liner: Sustainment-as-a-service for school districts and transit agencies stuck with electric buses whose manufacturer went bankrupt, using the military's orphan-platform playbook (salvaged parts pool, configuration control, depot repair, availability guarantees).
customer: School districts, regional education service agencies and small transit agencies that own buses from failed OEMs (Lion Electric US buses, Proterra, and similar EV truck and bus makers), plus state grant administrators and cooperative-purchasing bodies that want the taxpayer-funded fleets running.
problem: When Lion Electric went through bankruptcy and its new owner voided prior U.S. warranties, districts were left with buses nobody would service. Some sourced parts themselves, some sidelined buses, and some went back to diesel. Proterra's transit business went through a similar handoff. Grant-funded buses that sit idle are a political and audit embarrassment. Dealers cannot fix proprietary battery, inverter and charge-port faults, and there is no parts channel.
solution: Run it like a military orphan-platform sustainment program. (1) Buy the bankruptcy estate's remaining parts, tooling and diagnostics at liquidation. (2) Build a per-VIN configuration database and a reverse-engineered diagnostic library. (3) Stand up a regional depot and a mobile repair van for line-replaceable units: contactors, DC-DC converters, charge ports, battery management modules and pack modules. (4) Buy sidelined orphan buses cheaply as cannibalization donors. (5) Sell a fixed annual sustainment contract per bus that guarantees a morning-route availability rate, backed by a shared spares pool across districts sized with readiness-based sparing math.
why_now: Lion's sale voided U.S. warranties (reported late 2025), so the 2025-26 school year is when the pain became real. The installed base of grant-funded EV buses is large and aging out of warranty, and subsidy rollbacks (the federal commercial clean vehicle credit ended for vehicles acquired after Sept 30, 2025) make further OEM failures likely. The parts estates of failed makers are cheapest to buy right now, before anyone else sees their value.
revenue_model: Annual sustainment contract of roughly $4-8k per bus with an availability guarantee, plus time-and-materials for depot repairs, spares-pool membership fees for districts that want priority access, and salvage and refurbished battery pack sales. Sold through cooperative purchasing vehicles so districts do not each run a bid.
non_obvious_insight: Orphaned does not mean unfixable. In most orphaned fleets, 5-10 recurring line-replaceable units cause most of the downtime. A small shared spares pool plus a configuration-controlled baseline can lift availability from a coin flip to about 90%. The right buyer is not one district's bus garage but a state agency or regional service center pooling many districts, because the sparing math only works at fleet-of-fleets scale. Military sustainers call this the DMSMS problem and solved it by owning the baseline instead of waiting for the OEM.
first_30_days: Build a list of about 20 districts that took Lion or similar deliveries in 2022-24 from press coverage and grant award lists. Offer one district a free 'orphan health check' on a stranded bus using generic diagnostic tools and an EV-experienced transit mechanic. Register as a bidder in the relevant bankruptcy and liquidation processes and ask for the parts inventory lists. Hire 1-2 retired transit or heavy-duty EV technicians. Sign three districts to a per-bus quarterly pilot and use their fault logs to identify the top recurring failure modes.

title: Blind Validation Enclaves for Clinical AI
one_liner: Confidential-computing sandboxes where a hospital's private patient data and a vendor's private model meet, and only a signed performance report leaves.
customer: Health-system AI governance committees and health-AI vendors (imaging, ambient scribes, risk models), plus payers and insurers of AI performance guarantees.
problem: Hospitals cannot validate vendor claims on their own patients because PHI cannot leave and vendors will not ship weights. Published metrics rarely transfer to local populations. The Joint Commission and the Coalition for Health AI issued responsible-AI guidance in Sept 2025 and planned voluntary certification, so buyers now need evidence.
solution: A managed enclave (confidential VMs and GPUs) deployed in the hospital's own cloud tenant. The vendor's container runs against local retrospective data. Attestation proves that the evaluation code was unmodified and nothing was exfiltrated. The output is a signed report on subgroup performance, calibration and drift, repeated quarterly as post-deployment monitoring.
why_now: Confidential GPUs became generally available on major clouds in 2025, health systems adopted ambient scribes and imaging AI at scale, and Joint Commission and CHAI guidance created a demand for third-party assurance. The vendor-paid validation model is visibly conflicted.
revenue_model: $25-75k per validation (split between hospital and vendor), $10k per quarter monitoring, and payer or insurer programmes.
non_obvious_insight: Neither party trusts the other with its crown jewel, and the usual referee (the vendor) is conflicted. A machine that both sides can cryptographically verify replaces the trusted third party, so the product is the attestation as much as the test.
first_30_days: Partner with one academic medical centre's informatics team and two imaging or scribe vendors for a single use-case pilot. Use an existing confidential-computing offering rather than building infrastructure.

title: Owner-Statement Auditor for Landlords With Property Managers
one_liner: Forward your property manager's monthly owner statements and get back the line items that don't add up: repairs with no invoice, charges on the wrong property, reserve draws that hide shortfalls, and true days vacant.
customer: Self-directed small investors with 2 to 30 doors who pay a third-party property manager, especially out-of-state owners. A second tier is the bookkeepers and CPAs who serve them and would white-label it.
problem: Every PM uses a different statement format, a different definition of 'net to owner' and a different fee schedule. Owners cannot tell whether a $400 repair really cost $900. Fees are often a percentage of the project, so the PM benefits from a bigger job. Thorough reconciliation takes 5 to 10 minutes per property per month, so most owners only glance at the deposit. Owners with several PMs end up rebuilding everything in QuickBooks or Excel by hand.
solution: An email-in service with no new PM software. The owner forwards PDF or CSV statements, or connects the PM portal export. Document extraction normalizes each statement into one chart of accounts. The owner also uploads the PM agreement, and the service extracts its fee terms and approval thresholds. Rules then flag: charges with no invoice; repeated repairs just under the approval threshold; the same vendor billed across properties for work meant for one; reserve movements that mask a shortfall; late-fee handling that differs from the contract; and fees booked in the wrong month. It also computes true days vacant (turn time included) as opposed to the 'days on market' PMs report, plus maintenance cost per door and the share of work orders closed on the first visit. Output is a one-page monthly report and a ready-to-send dispute email. An optional human bookkeeper review is the upsell.
why_now: Sept 2026 BiggerPockets threads show owners asking these exact questions with no tool that answers them. Landlord banking tools (Baselane, RentRedi) still 'aren't really bookkeeping', as one thread puts it. Extracting structured data from messy PM statement PDFs became cheap and reliable with current document-AI models. That turns a manual forensic accounting service into a $9-per-door product.
revenue_model: $9 per door per month, or $99 per property per year. A one-time $199 backfill audit of the trailing 12 months acts as the lead magnet and first revenue. A bookkeeper and CPA white-label plan at about $49 per client per month. The audit could later be paired with recovery: for any overcharge that gets refunded, take 15%.
non_obvious_insight: Owners are not asking for another PM platform. They want a neutral second set of eyes, and PMs will never build one because they are the party being checked. Evidence: 'How do you verify your PM net deposit matches the statement each month?' (19 replies) lists wrong-property charges, repairs with no invoice, and reserve adjustments that absorb shortfalls, at 5-10 minutes per property (https://www.biggerpockets.com/forums/899/topics/1293899-how-do-you-verify-your-pm-net-deposit-matches-the-statement-each-month). 'Every PM seems to send a different statement format, a different definition of net to owner' (https://www.biggerpockets.com/forums/963/topics/1292833-owners-with-multiple-pms-how-do-you-keep-one-clean-view-across-statements). Owners can't verify whether a $400 repair needed $900, and 'days on market is not days vacant' (https://www.biggerpockets.com/forums/963/topics/1301673-what-actually-keeps-out-of-state-landlords-up-at-night). A repair-transparency survey quote reads: 'I couldn't tell which line items were fair and which were padded' (https://www.biggerpockets.com/forums/52/topics/1302340-small-landlords-with-a-pm-2-minute-survey-on-fees-and-repair-estimates).
first_30_days: Week 1: reply in the threads above and offer a free 12-month statement audit to 10 owners in exchange for anonymized statements. Build the audit by hand with a spreadsheet, an extraction prompt and a rules checklist. Weeks 2 to 3: deliver the audits, and use the discrepancies found as case studies. Week 4: convert to the $199 backfill and $9-per-door subscription, and pitch three real-estate bookkeepers on the white-label plan. Target: 10 paying owners and 2 bookkeeper partners.

title: Mitigation Grant Packets for Small Towns
one_liner: A packet factory and compliance tracker that gets small governments through FEMA and state mitigation grants without clawbacks.
customer: Municipalities under 25,000 people, counties, tribal governments, special districts and state emergency-management agencies, paid from management-cost lines.
problem: BRIC was cancelled in April 2025, restored by court order, reinstated Mar 18 2026 with $1B, and applications closed July 23 2026. Small governments lack staff for benefit-cost analysis, environmental and historic review, procurement and match documentation, and then risk clawbacks. California's new Safe Homes Grant and SB 894 revolving loan need local administration.
solution: Standardized templates for the top project types (culvert upsizing, generators, elevation, defensible space, floodproofing, safe rooms), covering benefit-cost analysis, environmental checklists and procurement. Add post-award compliance and drawdown tracking, built for several programs since BRIC timing is uncertain.
why_now: Federal funding restarted but is unstable. States are building their own programs, and big consultants ignore small jobs.
revenue_model: $6-20K fixed fee per packet and $1-2K/month compliance retainers.
non_obvious_insight: Government grants are gated by paperwork, and the volume of unserved demand sits in towns that big consultants skip.
first_30_days: Cold-email 200 town managers in high-hazard states with a free readiness scan, and sign 3 pilots.

title: Night Shift Tox Bulletin for Opioid Settlement Counties
one_liner: A no-patient-data network where rural ER nurses text in what they are seeing, turned into weekly local drug-supply alerts sold to counties spending opioid settlement money.
customer: County opioid settlement councils and public health departments, EMS medical directors, jails, harm-reduction programs and rural hospitals. Paid by county contract from opioid settlement funds.
problem: New adulterants show up in a rural ER as a pattern before they show up in any dataset. Examples are patients who are sedated but not responding to naloxone, or patients with a slow heart rate and low blood pressure that is not the usual opioid picture, or brutal withdrawal with high blood pressure. Confirmatory lab results take weeks or months. Surveillance networks are concentrated in academic and urban centers, so a rural county may learn about something two states over long after the ER has seen it. Nurses talk to each other in the break room and on private Facebook groups, but they have no safe way to alert the county, EMS, jail or harm-reduction workers. Hospital administrations do not want a nurse speaking for the hospital.
solution: A 30-second SMS or Signal report with no patient identifiers: date, county, number of patients, presentation flags, response to reversal, what the patients said they took, and any new physical findings such as wounds. Reports are aggregated with a minimum threshold (for example 3 or more per week) to protect privacy. The service returns a plain-language weekly county bulletin to nurses, EMS, jail medical staff and harm-reduction groups, and triggers targeted drug-checking or lab testing of residue with a lab partner. Include a jail-specific alert because withdrawal from newer sedatives is dangerous inside a jail.
why_now: Medetomidine, a veterinary sedative, is now in the illicit supply well beyond Philadelphia. Wastewater data showed it in at least one of 14 states every week from October 2025 to January 2026, and California published an emerging issue brief in April 2026. The main ER sentinel program has only about 17 to 20 academic centers, so rural emergency departments are barely covered. Tens of billions of dollars in opioid settlement funds are arriving in local hands, and county councils are actively looking for evidence-based data and surveillance projects.
revenue_model: $12-36k per year per county or multi-county region, with a lower price for small counties and bundled state contracts through state opioid settlement offices. A secondary product is a per-test fee when the network triggers drug-checking or lab confirmation, and a jail early-warning subscription.
non_obvious_insight: The scarce thing is not lab capacity. It is a trusted channel for the person who sees it first and has no authority to speak. A night-shift nurse is a better early-warning sensor than a dashboard, and the data is qualitative and deliberately human: 'this doesn't look like what we normally see.' Because you can build it with no PHI, nurses can contribute from their own phones off shift without touching hospital systems. Other tools (ODMAP, poison center feeds) are built for incident counts and law enforcement or EMS reports, not clinical pattern recognition.
first_30_days: Recruit 25 rural ER and night nurses from state nurses' groups and private Facebook communities. Send a free weekly bulletin to three neighboring counties and their EMS agencies. Attend an opioid settlement council meeting (agendas and minutes are public) in one of them. Offer a paid six-month pilot at $1,000 per month. Line up one lab partner for confirmatory testing. Get a lawyer to review the no-PHI reporting language and publish a clear policy telling nurses to leave out anything identifiable.

title: Cloud Machine Shop for High-School Shop Class
one_liner: Students design parts, watch real CNC machines cut them live at a partner job shop, and receive the parts by mail, so any school gets a hands-on manufacturing lab without machines or instructors.
customer: High-school and community-college CTE and robotics programs (per-project fees, often funded by CTE grants); job shops sponsor for recruiting.
problem: Manufacturing has openings, but CNC labs cost $100k+ and need instructors who are scarce, so rural and small schools cannot offer them. AI can now generate designs but students never touch real machining. Hands-on work is also the AI-resilient part of learning.
solution: A web portal: design in browser CAD with AI assist, automatic manufacturability checks and CAM by the partner shop, a scheduled live-stream slot where the machine cuts the student's part with a shop mentor narrating, then shipment. Curriculum aligns to entry-level machining credential levels and gives teachers a dashboard.
why_now: Text-to-CAD and instant-quote manufacturing platforms are good enough in 2026, streaming is trivial, and job shops have idle off-peak capacity and hiring pain. School AI pauses and screen fatigue make hands-on offerings attractive.
revenue_model: $25-60 per student project, $3-6k per classroom per year, plus recruiting sponsorship from job shops and manufacturer associations.
non_obvious_insight: Equipment and instructors are the constraint, not student interest. Machines already run from files, so the lab can be teleported, and idle night-shift capacity is a free asset that the shop's hiring pain will pay to use.
first_30_days: Partner with one local job shop with a couple of machines available off-peak. Recruit 5 CTE or robotics teachers. Run a 3-week design-and-cut unit at $30 per student and measure engagement. Map the unit to a machining credential standard.

title: Mini Cat Bonds for Co-ops and Counties
one_liner: Cat bond capital is at record highs but deals under $50M are uneconomic. Make a $5-25M cat bond a 90-day, low-cost, template product for the sponsors the market ignores.
customer: Small public risk pools, rural electric cooperatives, counties, hospital systems and small regional insurers needing $5M-$50M of catastrophe protection.
problem: Cat bond issuance is a record $18.9B year to date with $65.6B outstanding, yet legal, modeling, rating and SPV costs of $1M-plus put small deals out of reach. Small sponsors stay in the traditional market or go bare, while primary property markets stay hard.
solution: A standardized private cat bond or collateralized reinsurance template: pre-approved documents, standard parametric triggers with an independent calculation agent, treasury-fund collateral with transparent accounting, and a target all-in cost under $150k with issuance in about 90 days. Sell the notes to ILS funds seeking diversification.
why_now: Record traditional and ILS capital, softening through 2027 (Jefferies), and mature tokenized and money-market collateral (Goldman put a $100B Treasury fund into crypto plumbing, CoinDesk 2026-09-28). ILS investors want diversification beyond Florida wind.
revenue_model: 1.5-3% of limit as a structuring fee, plus annual administration and calculation-agent fees.
non_obvious_insight: Softening means capital wants to deploy, so the binding constraint is deal cost per dollar of limit. That is a documentation and operations problem, not a risk-appetite problem.
first_30_days: Retain an offshore law firm and a calculation agent. Find two state pooling associations with wildfire or hail exposure, get indications of interest from two ILS funds, and produce a reusable term-sheet template. Charge a structuring retainer to fund first-deal work.

title: Outsourced 24-Hour Vulnerability Reporting Desk (CRA)
one_liner: A retainer service that acts as the manufacturer's PSIRT: it watches for actively exploited vulnerabilities in their products' components and files the 24-hour early warning, follow-up notification and final report to the EU platform.
customer: Connected-device makers with 20-500 employees selling into the EU with no 24/7 security team: smart home, e-bikes and scooters, industrial sensors, routers, wearables, toys, EV chargers. Many are non-EU (US and Asian) firms.
problem: CRA reporting obligations began 11 Sep 2026: 24-hour reporting to ENISA for actively exploited vulnerabilities and severe incidents, with fines up to EUR 15M or 2.5% of turnover. Small makers have no on-call rota, no SBOM monitoring and no idea what 'actively exploited' means for their firmware. The briefing found almost no visible tooling aimed at them.
solution: A retainer that ingests each product's SBOM per firmware version, matches it continuously against exploited-vulnerability and threat feeds, triages 24/7 with a pre-agreed decision tree, and files the early warning, notification and final report with text approved by the client's named contact. It also runs coordinated disclosure and advisory publishing, plus quarterly tabletop drills. Software lets one analyst cover 30+ clients.
why_now: The reporting duty went live 17 days ago and the full regime follows in Dec 2027. Firms are discovering that the deadline is a staffing problem, not a document problem.
revenue_model: EUR 1,500-6,000/month retainer, incident surcharges, and EUR 5k annual tabletop exercises.
non_obvious_insight: A 24-hour clock makes this a staffing obligation, which small firms cannot meet alone but a pooled desk can, like outsourced DPO services. Each reported vulnerability also gives a natural upsell into SBOM and technical-file work.
first_30_days: Partner with two or three EU security consultancies or product-safety associations. Sell a EUR 2.5k one-day 'CRA reporting readiness audit' to 20 firms, convert 5-8 into EUR 2k/month retainers, and contract three part-time analysts across time zones.

title: Pickleball Courts Inside Empty Fellowship Halls
one_liner: A turnkey operator that converts congregations' idle gyms and fellowship halls into revenue-sharing indoor pickleball venues, with lines, nets, insurance and booking handled.
customer: Congregations (churches, synagogues, mosques, temples) with a gym or hall and parking lot, who receive a rent share. Players (often retirees on weekday mornings) pay $8-15 per session.
problem: US pickleball grew from 13.6M (2023) to 24.3M (2025) players, but courts are scarce (about 1 dedicated court per 1,000 participants in the Mid-Atlantic, and about $900M of investment needed per a 2022 SFIA report). Outdoor courts are being restricted or closed by noise complaints. Meanwhile congregations that are shrinking or flat (only 33% of Americans attend monthly) sit on large rooms used a few hours a week, and fear liability and tax surprises.
solution: A standard hall kit (removable court lines, portable nets, wall padding, ball machine), a legal and insurance package (lease template, additional-insured wording, a flat-rent structure designed to avoid UBIT problems, waivers), a booking app with open-play scheduling and rating-linked sessions, and part-time paid hosts. Indoor play removes the neighbor-noise problem.
why_now: Participation more than doubled in two years, and noise fights are closing outdoor courts (Kirkwood MO, Walnut Creek CA, Halifax). Church rental-liability gaps are a known insurance pain point. Congregations need non-donation income.
revenue_model: Player fees of $10-14 per session. The congregation takes a 20-40% share and the operator keeps the rest less host cost. Kit rental or sale ($200/month or $3-5k) and an insurance-program commission.
non_obvious_insight: The court shortage is framed as a construction problem needing $900M. It is a liability and coordination problem: the courts already exist as 40x70 ft hardwood rooms with parking, owned by institutions that want steady income but cannot underwrite risk. A congregation is also a more trusted neighbor than a new commercial club.
first_30_days: Sign 3 congregations with gyms in one metro through denominational property committees and local pickleball Facebook groups. Run two open-play nights a week using a $1.5k kit. Pre-sell via local groups, track fill rate, and get a church-insurer quote. Aim for $1-2k revenue in the first month.

title: Master-Leased Housing to Recruit Care Workers Domestically
one_liner: Asset-light staff housing near care facilities that lets operators recruit domestic workers from a wider radius, starting with stranded worker apartments.
customer: Nursing homes, assisted-living and memory-care operators (5-40 sites) and home-care agencies in tight labor markets such as Wisconsin and rural areas.
problem: The visa pause cuts off the overseas pipeline. Direct care workers are paid little (66% earn under $35k), so domestic recruits can't afford to relocate to where beds are staffed. Closed beds and wings in Wisconsin show the cost. Turnover of 77-80% means every hire has to be retained.
solution: Master-lease or take over apartments near facilities, furnish them, and sublease bed by bed to employees at below-market rent. Employers fund the gap ($300-600 per bed per month) under a guarantee. Add a 3-month 'landing pad' with transport, CNA certification and ESL classes, and a relocation pipeline from oversupplied labor markets (laid-off retail and hospitality workers).
why_now: Wisconsin nursing homes spent $100k+ on apartments for overseas workers and then abandoned the plan when visa access closed, so there are stranded assets to take over. About 350,000 Haitians lost TPS on Aug 4, and about one in five immigrant direct-care workers come from countries hit by the 75-country visa pause.
revenue_model: Per-bed monthly management margin ($100-200 on top of rent), employer subsidy, and a $1,500 placement fee per hire retained at 90 days.
non_obvious_insight: When foreign labor is cut off, housing rather than wages becomes the binding constraint to domestic recruitment. A 20-bed closed wing loses over $1M a year in revenue, so a $7k a year housing subsidy per worker is trivially worth it.
first_30_days: Approach the Wisconsin operators who bought apartments and offer to operate and re-let them to domestic hires. Run a 12-bed pilot in one town with two operators and track time-to-fill and 90-day retention.

title: Mailed Proof Books for Grandparents Who Buy Prints
one_liner: Turn a wedding gallery into a personalized printed booklet, mailed to each grandparent and parent with a phone number to order prints, because the people who actually pay for wedding prints never click gallery links.
customer: Wedding photographers (they pay only via revenue share). The end payers are the couple's parents, in-laws and grandparents, who spend $150-400 per household on prints and albums.
problem: The dirty secret of studio economics is that couples buy almost nothing after delivery. They have the gallery and Instagram. The people who buy prints and albums are mothers, mothers-in-law and grandparents, and the photographer's only delivery channel is a link emailed to the couple, who rarely forward it. Pic-Time and similar platforms added face-recognition and selfie-search galleries in late 2025, but that assumes a phone-comfortable guest willing to scan their face on a website. Grandma will not do that. Every wedding leaves an estimated $500-2,000 of print revenue uncollected, and the 'last photo with Grandpa' has a clock on it.
solution: The photographer uploads the gallery and the family list (they already have it from the formals shot list). We cluster faces, have the photographer confirm the 6-12 key elders and parents, and auto-build a 16-24 page softcover booklet per person ('Nana's Book: 22 photos of you and your grandkids'). We print and mail it within about 10 days of gallery delivery, with the couple's opt-in and a handwritten-style note from them. Every booklet carries a QR code plus a toll-free number answered first by a human and later by a voice agent that takes orders by phone and card, with check-by-mail as an option. Orders are fulfilled through pro labs, and the photographer sees a dashboard of sales.
why_now: AI face search has just become standard in photographer gallery platforms (Pic-Time's Nov 2025 update), which proves photographers will pay for AI galleries but leaves the elder channel unserved. Softcover print-on-demand now lands at roughly $6-10 for a 24-page book via lab and POD APIs. 2026-grade voice agents can take a print order from a 78-year-old who hates websites. Wedding-guest demographics are also aging, since couples are marrying later and grandparents are still at the table.
revenue_model: No upfront fee to the photographer. We front the booklet cost (about $10 landed) and keep roughly 40% of resulting print and album order revenue at lab retail, with the photographer keeping 60%, which is pure incremental margin. Optional $15 flat per-booklet pricing for photographers who want to buy outright.
non_obvious_insight: The buyer is not the client. The couple's inbox is the wrong channel, and a personalized object with the recipient's own face on it is something people do not throw away. The product is a channel to 60-85-year-olds who respond to paper and phone calls, and the gallery software is just the data source.
first_30_days: Recruit 10 photographers from local and online groups who delivered a wedding in the last 6 months. Produce booklets for 2 of their weddings each, at your cost (about $100 in print and postage per wedding), using a Pic-Time/ShootProof export, open-source face clustering (InsightFace) and a lab or Lulu/Blurb-style API. Route the phone number to the founder's cell. Track orders per booklet. If 1 in 5 booklets converts to a $100+ order, sign the rev-share terms and scale to 50 studios.

title: Retrain Displaced Managers for Data-Center Builds
one_liner: A 10-week bridge program that turns laid-off program managers, analysts and ops leads into project-controls, cost-estimating, commissioning-paperwork and permitting roles at data-center and grid builders.
customer: General contractors, EPC firms, data-center developers and utility contractors pay a $12-25k placement fee or staff-augmentation margin. Learners pay little, or the cost is covered by workforce-board funds.
problem: Everyone tells displaced office workers to 'learn AI', the most crowded direction. Meanwhile AI's own physical build-out has a shortage of schedulers (P6), cost engineers, document controllers, commissioning coordinators and interconnection or permit analysts. Contractors can't hire them, and mid-career office workers face 6-13 month searches.
solution: Cohort training on scheduling, cost control, contracts, commissioning documentation and site-safety basics, taught by retired project-controls leads. It includes a paid 4-week job-shadow on live projects, certification prep (OSHA 30, PMI-SP, AACE) and guaranteed interviews with partner contractors.
why_now: Hyperscaler capex on data centers and grid work is at record levels and contractors openly cite labor shortages. Big-company cuts of managers ('anti-bureaucracy' layoffs like Amazon's ~16,000) are pushing experienced coordinators onto the market. Stanford data shows the pain concentrated in AI-exposed office roles.
revenue_model: Placement fee of 10-15% of first-year salary (about $12-18k) from contractors, plus paid corporate cohorts and optional deferred tuition.
non_obvious_insight: The AI boom creates a shortage of non-technical, non-AI office roles in the physical world. The displaced manager's scarce skill (vendor wrangling, org navigation, documentation discipline) is exactly what construction lacks, and nobody is training for it.
first_30_days: Call 20 mid-size mechanical and electrical contractors in hot markets (Texas, Virginia, Ohio, Arizona) and get their unfilled-role lists. Sign 3 pay-per-hire LOIs. Recruit 15 laid-off PMs from layoff communities. Run a 4-week evening pilot with a retired scheduler and place the first 5.

title: The Recorder's Rulebook: Avalara for the Recording Counter
one_liner: A verified, machine-readable rulebook and fee oracle for every recording jurisdiction, with a preflight checker that tells you a document will be rejected before you send it.
customer: Small and mid-size title and escrow agencies, estate-planning and real estate attorneys, HOA and property managers, lenders' closing teams, and later closing-software and e-recording platforms that embed the API. Counties get listed free.
problem: There are roughly 3,600 recording jurisdictions, each with its own margins, font sizes, notary wording, parcel-ID format, cover sheets, per-page fees, surcharges and transfer taxes. Those rules sit on stale county web pages and in clerks' heads. Rejections delay closings two to seven days, burn recorder staff time on every bounce, and wrong fee estimates create TRID tolerance problems for lenders. Fees also keep moving as counties backfill shrinking recording revenue (Wayne County MI has floated a $30 fee increase, Montana raised per-page fees, and other counties report seven-figure losses tied to fee changes).
solution: A crowd-verified rulebook per county and document type. A PDF preflight scans geometry (margins, fonts, blank space), notary block completeness, legal description, APN format and preparer and return-to fields, and returns specific fixes. A to-the-penny fee and transfer-tax calculator handles every surcharge. A change log tracks statute changes and effective dates (many take effect July 1 or January 1). Each county gets a one-click quarterly 'attest my page' link, which clerks will use because every rejection costs them 15-30 minutes plus postage. Start as a free 'will this be rejected?' web checker to collect users, then sell API access.
why_now: Recording volumes have been depressed since 2022 and counties are raising fees, which makes fee tables stale. Remote online notarization and e-recording put far more documents in front of closers who have never met the county's quirks. Title staff attrition means fewer people who just know the rules. Vision-capable LLMs make geometry and notary-block checks cheap for the first time.
revenue_model: $1-$3 per preflight check plus $99-$499/month tiers for agencies. Per-call API pricing for closing platforms and e-recording vendors, and a data license for lenders needing accurate recording-fee and transfer-tax estimates.
non_obvious_insight: Clerks reject because the stamp is a legal act, not because we are picky. The top ten rejection reasons are identical everywhere, but the thresholds differ, and most bounces come from occasional submitters (attorneys, HOA managers, individuals), not the big title companies that already have local runners. The moat is not software, it is the boring verified dataset, and clerks will help you build it because they are the ones who suffer from the bounces.
first_30_days: Pick one state with an active recorders' association and build the full rulebook for 25 counties by phone and web, with a clerk sign-off on each. Ship the free checker, promote it through the association newsletter and estate-planning attorney groups, and convert the heaviest users to a $99/month plan. Approach a closing-software partner program once you have about 200 active users.

title: Shoot-Out Co-Own: Legal OS for Friend Homebuyers
one_liner: A co-ownership package for friend groups: a state-specific ownership agreement with a built-in Texas-shoot-out buyout, contribution-weighted equity, default rules and lender-friendly structure.
customer: Groups of 2-4 unrelated Gen Z and younger-millennial earners (friend pods, siblings, single buyers) in high-cost metros, referred by buyers' agents, mortgage brokers and credit unions.
problem: Surveys show roughly a third of Gen Z considering co-buying and about 60% of renters open to it, yet actual co-buying is rare because it is legally scary. What if someone wants out, marries, loses a job or dies? Lenders and title companies improvise, and disputes end friendships. First-time buyers now reach ownership around age 40, so the pressure to pool is real.
solution: A standardized co-ownership stack: a state-specific tenancy-in-common or LLC agreement, a scheduled shoot-out exit (one owner names a price, the others must buy or sell at it, which forces a fair price without appraisals or lawsuits), rights of first refusal, contribution-weighted equity with cure-period and dilution remedies for missed payments, and a shared sinking fund. It includes a multi-borrower mortgage broker network and a ledger that tracks each owner's cash and sweat equity. Life-event amendments handle marriage, job loss and death.
why_now: Co-buying interest is at record highs in 2026 surveys (Bank of America found about 32% of Gen Z considering it, and Rocket found about 60% of renters considering it), while median first-time buyer age hit a record near 40 in 2025. Lenders are courting co-borrowers and there is no dominant standard exit document.
revenue_model: $1,500-$3,000 per group for the legal package, $15 per month for the ledger and reminders, $1,000-$2,500 referral fees per funded loan, title and insurance affiliate fees, and a 1% fee to administer a shoot-out at exit.
non_obvious_insight: The friction is not wanting to co-buy, it is the exit. A shoot-out clause borrowed from partnership law gives every co-owner a fair way out and doubles as price discovery. Whoever owns the standard exit template becomes the SAFE-note of co-ownership.
first_30_days: Partner with five buyers' agents and two mortgage brokers in high-cost metros such as Seattle, Denver, Boston and the Bay Area. Recruit friend groups from first-time-buyer and house-hacking communities. Have a real-estate attorney draft templates for two states. Sell 10 pilot packages at $1,500, refunded if the deal does not close.

title: Data Act Broker for Equipment Owners
one_liner: File and operationalize EU Data Act data-access demands so independent service shops can finally read the diagnostics that elevator, heat-pump, forklift and tractor makers lock away.
customer: Independent maintenance and service companies in the EU (starting with elevator/escalator maintainers, then commercial heat-pump installers, forklift and ag-machinery shops). They pay per monitored asset per month. Equipment-owning businesses (building managers, hospitals, logistics sites) are the secondary payer, because they hold the legal right.
problem: Original manufacturers use exclusive access to machine diagnostics and fault logs to keep 60-80% of the lucrative service market. Independents work blind, so they lose contracts to OEMs. The EU Data Act (applicable since 12 Sep 2025) gives the user of a connected product, including a business, the right to get the data the product generates. The user can also have it handed to any third party of their choice. In practice almost nobody exercises the right. The paperwork is unfamiliar, OEMs stall, and the data arrives in a different format from every vendor.
solution: An agency-plus-plumbing service. (1) Sign a user-authorization letter with the equipment owner. (2) Auto-generate and file the Article 4/5 access and third-party-sharing requests to each OEM and track statutory response deadlines. (3) Ingest whatever comes back, whether an API, a file dump or a portal export. (4) Normalize it into one cross-vendor schema per asset class. (5) Give the independent shop a fleet-health dashboard and fault-prediction alerts. Add a public compliance scorecard showing which OEMs comply, and escalate the ones that do not to national enforcement authorities.
why_now: The Data Act became applicable on 12 Sep 2025. On 12 Sep 2026, 16 days ago, its design obligation started applying to newly placed connected products, so data must be accessible by default. The right-to-repair movement is at peak momentum. OEM stonewalling now generates complaints that regulators must act on. No one has industrialized user-side requests yet, so the first mover sets the standard schema and templates.
revenue_model: Setup fee of about 50-150 EUR per asset for the request and integration work, plus 4-12 EUR per asset per month for the normalized feed and health analytics. Add-ons: predictive-maintenance alerts and a white-label owner portal. Later: sell anonymized cross-fleet reliability benchmarks to insurers and asset owners.
non_obvious_insight: A legal right is worthless until someone industrializes exercising it. The Data Act gives the data-access key to the owner, not the repairer, so the winning business acts as the owner's agent and sells the result to the repairer. The moat is accumulated request templates, OEM-by-OEM response knowledge, and one normalized schema. Every OEM refusal also becomes evidence for regulators, which turns compliance friction into marketing.
first_30_days: Pick one vertical and one country pair, for example independent elevator maintainers in Germany and the Netherlands, and reach them through trade associations. Retain a Data Act lawyer for a fixed fee to finalize request templates. Recruit 5 independent shops, get user-authorization letters covering about 50 units, and file the requests. Log every OEM response and format. Charge a pilot fee of about 1-2k EUR per shop for delivered data plus a first fleet report. Publish an OEM response-time tracker to build inbound demand. Expect uneven enforcement, so keep the pilot to OEMs that respond and use the ones that stonewall as regulator evidence.

title: Licensed True Stories for Narration Channels
one_liner: A story studio that interviews real people about real events and licenses the recordings and scripts to faceless story-narration channels, replacing scraped Reddit posts and fake AI-written 'confessions'.
customer: Operators of faceless YouTube, TikTok and podcast channels that narrate AITA-style, revenge, workplace and relationship-drama stories, from solo operators to 10-person studios, plus audio-drama and story apps. They pay roughly $40-$150 per non-exclusive license.
problem: These channels' supply is scraped Reddit posts they don't own, since authors keep copyright and Reddit's data licenses go to AI firms, not YouTubers. YouTube's July 2025 'inauthentic content' rules specifically flag readings of material not created by the uploader and templated narrated stories, and in January 2026 YouTube terminated 16 channels with 35M combined subscribers. Mods keep banning reposts and fabricated or AI-written stories, so fresh, real material is drying up. Freelancers on Fiverr write fake 'Reddit stories' for $10-$30 that read as obvious slop.
solution: A 15-minute voice-interview app plus a human editor. The storyteller tells their story out loud, and the studio transcribes and structures it into a narration-ready script with a signed release, ID check and revenue share. Channels get a non-exclusive or exclusive license and a 'voice-verified first-person account' provenance certificate they can show as original-source proof. Authors earn a share of licensed views through tracked license codes. Storytellers are recruited off Reddit so mods aren't disrupted.
why_now: YouTube's inauthentic-content policy took effect on 15 July 2025 and was followed by the January 2026 termination wave, so channel operators now need defensible originality and provenance. At the same time AI-written fake stories have flooded the genre, and mods removing them has shrunk the pool of scrapeable real material.
revenue_model: $40-$150 per non-exclusive license, $300-$800 for exclusive first-run, and bundles such as $499 per month for 10 licenses. Authors get 40-50% of revenue. Later, sell format and option rights to audio-drama and TV producers.
non_obvious_insight: Buyers are not short of scripts but of defensible originality. People tell true stories brilliantly out loud and badly in writing, so the audio-interview format both raises quality and creates a provenance signal that a text LLM can't cheaply fake. Mods know the top-performing genres and that the people who post these stories mostly do it for validation, not money, so a paid $30 interview is an easy yes.
first_30_days: Recruit 30 storytellers through Facebook groups, Craigslist and small creator ads at $30 per story. Produce 60 scripts with Whisper transcription plus human editing. Sell a $199 pilot pack of 10 stories to 20 narration-channel operators, found through public channel emails and faceless-creator Discords. Ask for view data on the first videos to validate the revenue-share model, and use the results as the pitch for subscription bundles.

title: IEP-Ready Adaptive Hardware, Printed to Order
one_liner: A micro-manufacturer that acts as the approved vendor for special-education adaptive hardware, starting with custom AAC keyguards for tablets and expanding to OT-prescribed grips, switch mounts and positioning aids.
customer: School district special-ed and assistive-technology coordinators, school SLPs and OTs, and private pediatric therapy clinics, paid through district purchase orders funded by IEP obligations.
problem: Free keyguard designs exist, and Etsy sellers make standard ones. But an SLP has no time to print, a district can't pay an Etsy seller by purchase order, and a custom AAC grid on a specific tablet and case needs an exact fit. Legally required AT then arrives weeks late. Every tablet or case refresh orphans last year's keyguards.
solution: A catalog and a 48-hour custom service. The SLP uploads a screenshot of the AAC layout and the tablet and case model. We return a fit-verified keyguard with an IEP-friendly quote and invoice. Then expand to OT-prescribed items (pencil grips, adaptive handles, switch and tablet mounts, tactile schedule boards) using a clinician-approved parametric library. Paperwork arrives ready for the file: W-9, liability insurance, net-30 terms and cooperative-purchasing listings.
why_now: Consumer-grade printing is now reliable enough for small runs of durable parts. Tablet-based AAC is now standard practice, and app grid layouts are standardized enough to parametrize. Districts are under pressure to meet AT obligations with tight budgets. Open-source designs prove the demand but leave the procurement gap wide open.
revenue_model: Per item ($35 to $95 for keyguards; $10 to $150 for other adaptive items), plus an annual district 'AT Bench' subscription ($3k to $8k covering a set number of custom items and a design consult).
non_obvious_insight: The scarce thing isn't the printing or even the design, since clinicians will share designs for free. It's the procurement wrapper: being a vendor a district can legally and easily pay. Whoever holds 'approved vendor' status with a few purchasing cooperatives gets pulled into every district's AT budget. Print cost is $4 against a $80 to $150 price because the customer is paying for zero-friction compliance and clinical fit.
first_30_days: Take the open-source keyguard parametric files and verify fit against the five most common tablet and case combinations. Post in SLP and AT groups: 'send a screenshot of your layout, first keyguard at cost, PO accepted.' Complete vendor registration with two districts and apply to one purchasing cooperative. Target 15 paid orders and one district relationship.

title: Fresh-Fall Meteorite Alerts and Landowner Desk
one_liner: Turn satellite lightning-sensor fireball detections into strewn-field maps within an hour, then broker signed landowner access and sale terms for hunters and dealers who pay for a 24-hour head start.
customer: Serious meteorite hunters, dealers and collectors (a few thousand worldwide), with museums and labs as secondary buyers of fresh, uncontaminated samples.
problem: Value depends on freshness and documentation. A witnessed fall recovered before rain sells for many times the price per gram of desert finds, and in my recollection a Martian meteorite sold for about $5.3M at auction in 2025. Hunters race using scattered social posts and public bolide feeds that arrive late. Landowners own the meteorites in the US, so the hunter who lands the landowner's yes wins.
solution: A pipeline that ingests public geostationary lightning-mapper fireball detections, weather-radar falling-debris signatures and upper-air winds to publish a dark-flight strewn ellipse in minutes. It overlays parcel data and gives the desk a landowner script, a one-page finder-landowner split contract, and a provenance dossier (time, coordinates, radar and satellite evidence) that raises sale price. Paid subscribers get the alert first.
why_now: GOES-19 became the operational eastern US geostationary satellite in 2025, with lightning imagers now covering the Americas and, as I understand it, Europe and East Asia. Open radar data is on the cloud, and the collectibles market is at extremes (a $16.5M single card in Feb 2026). LLM pipelines make a two-person alerting desk feasible.
revenue_model: $15 per month for hunter alerts, a $49 event pass for high-value falls, and 10% of sale value on brokered recoveries. Dealers pay about $300 per month for a priority feed and the landowner contract kit.
non_obvious_insight: Detection is free public data. The scarce input is speed to a signed landowner agreement before rain and rivals arrive. The business is a contracts-and-logistics desk that happens to run on satellite data, and the provenance dossier is the price multiplier.
first_30_days: Script the public fireball feeds and backtest on 2021-2025 falls. Open a Discord with 200 hunters and 5 dealers, and pre-sell 30 annual passes at $99. Offer to run the next credible fall end to end using the contract template, taking a percentage only if material is recovered.

title: Designed Toxin Binders for Mouse-Free Antivenom QC
one_liner: Sequence-defined, AI-designed toxin-class binders sold as reference reagents that let antivenom makers test potency without mouse lethality assays.
customer: Antivenom manufacturers (public institutes in Latin America and India, plus private and UK/US firms), WHO and regulator working groups, toxinology labs, and funders such as Wellcome and Gates for later recombinant antivenom.
problem: WHO's 2017 guidelines say murine LD50 and ED50 lethality tests remain the only validated preclinical potency method, despite 3Rs pressure. ELISA, nAChR-binding and cytotoxicity surrogates exist but lack stable, defined, universal reagents, because animal-derived antibodies vary lot to lot.
solution: Produce designed binders for the major toxin families (three-finger toxins, PLA2, SVMP) in E. coli, following the approach in Nature (Jan 2025), where de novo proteins neutralized three-finger toxins and protected mice. Sell (1) calibrator and capture-reagent kits for competition ELISA and nAChR-competition assays, and (2) a 'toxin-family neutralization profile' service showing what each antivenom lot neutralizes, correlated to mouse ED50 over 10-20 lots. Later, co-develop recombinant cocktails.
why_now: The 2025 Nature paper proved designed proteins can neutralize venom toxins. WHO explicitly encourages alternatives. Regulators are moving toward non-animal methods (FDA's Sept 21, 2026 rule is the latest signal). AI design has made binders cheap.
revenue_model: $2-10k research-use kits, $5-20k per lot profile service, grants ($200k-2M) for validation, and later per-dose royalties on recombinant products.
non_obvious_insight: Everyone frames designed antivenom as a therapeutic moonshot. The wedge is quality control: reagents sell before regulators accept a replacement, and manufacturers already pay for mouse colonies. Sequence-defined reagents beat animal-derived ones on reproducibility. Honest caveat: first revenue is likely grants plus small reagent orders.
first_30_days: Check IP with the University of Washington and DTU or design new binders. Express three binders. Send sample sets to 2 antivenom labs for correlation on 10 lots. Apply for a small grant while selling research-use kits to toxinology labs.

title: Leak-Proof Outsourcing Passport for Game Studios
one_liner: Contractor identity checks at first build access, per-recipient build watermarking and reusable vendor security attestations for the outsourcing chain (art, audio, QA, porting) that leaks unreleased games.
customer: Mid-size and AA/indie publishers that outsource to 20-200 external vendors. Also the vendors themselves (art studios in Poland, Vietnam, India and elsewhere, QA houses, localization and voice studios, freelance marketplaces) who need a portable credential to win work.
problem: Layoffs and cost-cutting push more production to external vendors and freelancers. Per the briefing, Ubisoft headcount fell from 18,666 to 16,590 and EA's $55B buyout, which closed 4 Aug 2026, aims to cut operating costs by putting AI throughout. Each vendor has weaker security than the publisher while unreleased builds are the crown jewels (GTA VI launches 19 Nov 2026, and past leaks like Rockstar 2022, Insomniac 2023 and Game Freak 2024 show the pattern). Remote contractors are also prime targets for identity fraud: North Korean IT-worker schemes hit 'nearly 70' and 'over 100' US companies in cases sentenced in Apr-May 2026, using deepfake-assisted interviews and stolen identities. Film has the MPA's Trusted Partner Network; games have no equivalent.
solution: A subscription 'passport' with five parts. (1) Contractor identity verification with liveness and injection-attack detection at onboarding and again at first privileged build access, tied to device posture. (2) A game-specific vendor security attestation, evidence-based (SSO, endpoint, repo hygiene) and shared across publishers so a vendor is assessed once. (3) Per-recipient forensic watermarking of builds, assets and design documents so a leak can be traced to a person or vendor. (4) Offboarding automation for contract end or layoff waves. (5) Insurer-ready evidence packages for cyber and E&O cover.
why_now: EA's leveraged buyout, Ubisoft's restructuring and Tencent-backed Vantage carve-out are all driving outsourcing. GTA VI's launch date will attract extortion attempts. North Korean IT-worker cases and deepfake interview kits make hiring-time identity checks insufficient. The IDScan.net breach (153M license scans) makes zero-retention verification a selling point (per briefing), and enterprise identity products are crowded but none focus on game supply chains.
revenue_model: Publishers pay $1.5-6k/month plus $30-80 per contractor-month. Vendors pay $200-500/month for a portable attestation badge, giving vendor-pays adoption. Watermarking priced per build distribution.
non_obvious_insight: The bottleneck is not the publisher's own security but that each publisher re-audits the same few hundred vendors. A shared 'assess once, reuse everywhere' passport (film's TPN model) is cheaper for publishers and turns vendors into paying customers. Identity must be verified at the moment of privileged access rather than at hiring, because proxy interviews and deepfakes defeat interview-time checks.
first_30_days: Partner with 2-3 mid-size publishers or a co-dev/QA outsourcer. Draft a 40-question game-specific assessment, wire up an existing IDV API plus a device-posture check, and pilot with one outsourcing vendor. Offer a 'leak-trace drill' using watermarks on a demo build. Sell to publishers' security leads at $1.5k/month pilots.

title: Data Centers Fund Neighborhood Batteries in Emerging Cities
one_liner: Sell data-center developers in capacity-starved emerging cities a bring-your-own-capacity package delivered as batteries and solar at nearby small businesses, dispatched to the local utility at the evening peak.
customer: Colocation and edge data-center developers (5-100 MW) in cities such as Nairobi, Lagos, Johannesburg, Cape Town, Johor and Sao Paulo.
problem: Data-center projects are stalling on power and social license: Equinix's Cape Town plan (174 MW, 4.4B liters of water a year) drew protests and Kenya's 1 GW G42-Microsoft project is stalled. Utilities cannot add capacity quickly, gas turbines are sold out through 2029-30 at about $2,157/kW, and PJM now makes large loads bring their own capacity or curtail. In emerging cities, nearby small businesses already suffer outages and run diesel gensets.
solution: An aggregator finances 1-5 MWh of C&I batteries and solar at hundreds of businesses near the data center's substation (cold rooms, clinics, schools, bakeries, malls), with leases funded by the data center's capacity fee. The businesses get outage protection, and 20-30% of each battery is reserved for evening-peak dispatch, metered and verified. The developer gets a firm capacity certificate for its utility filing and a community-benefit story: the neighborhood's evening peak falls and outages drop by a stated number of hours.
why_now: Bring-your-own-capacity is now the template (PJM's backstop auction and curtailment proposals, Voltus selling 100 MW to Google, Sunrun, Tesla and Renew Home pitching 16.8 GW of capacity-as-a-service). The Duke study shows flexibility could unlock 76 GW at 0.25% curtailment, stationary batteries are around $70/kWh, and the 100-500 kWh C&I band is underserved because suppliers set roughly 10 MW minimums.
revenue_model: A capacity fee from the data center, benchmarked to PJM's $325-555 per MW-day (roughly $120-200 per kW-year) and to be validated locally, on 10-15 year terms, plus lease income from the small businesses and dispatch or demand-response revenue from the utility.
non_obvious_insight: The data center's real willingness to pay is set by the cost of delay (about $14M a month for an idle 60 MW site) and by permit risk, not by the value of the kWh. In emerging cities the marginal capacity is neighbors' diesel gensets, so replacing them with batteries is both the cheapest firm capacity and the way to defuse local opposition.
first_30_days: Pick one stuck project (a 20-50 MW edge or colo site in Nairobi, Lagos or Johannesburg), reach the developer's power or permitting lead, and propose a paid 500 kWh pilot. Sign 15-20 businesses within 3 km of the substation, log feeder evening-peak load before and after, and deliver a feeder-impact report as the pitch asset.

title: Reliance Ratings for SOC 2 Reports and Auditors
one_liner: A buyer-paid forensic desk that tells vendor-risk teams how far to trust a given SOC 2 or ISO report, and the audit firm that signed it.
customer: Third-party-risk and security teams at banks, health systems, insurers and mid-market SaaS companies that ingest hundreds of vendor reports a year. Cyber insurers and PE/VC diligence teams are the second wave.
problem: In March 2026 a whistleblower alleged that Delve, a YC-backed startup valued at about $300M, issued 494 near-identical SOC 2 reports with conclusions pre-filled and signed by two rubber-stamp firms. YC removed it in April, and Delve disputes the claims. Buyers now suspect every clean PDF. Manual checks of AICPA peer-review and NASBA licence records take about 30 minutes per report, so most teams skip them.
solution: The buyer uploads the vendor's report. We compare it with a growing corpus using fuzzy fingerprints of system descriptions, test procedures and exception language. We check CPA licence, AICPA peer-review status, firm ownership, address and staffing footprint, sample sizes, period length, carve-outs and subservice-organisation scope. Output is a reliance score, a one-page red-flag memo, and a continuously updated rating of audit firms based on exception rates, boilerplate share and peer-review opinions.
why_now: The Delve fallout in spring 2026 made every security team ask 'who signed this?'. Compliance-automation platforms now tie vendors to audit-firm networks at scale (Vanta reports about 16,000 customers). LLMs make reading and comparing thousands of 80-page reports cheap for the first time.
revenue_model: $200-400 per report on demand, $20-60k per year TPRM subscriptions, API licences to vendor-risk platforms, and insurer portfolio scans.
non_obvious_insight: Insiders treat the audit as a commodity input that automation has solved. Audit quality varies enormously and invisibly, and the vendor pays its own auditor. That is the same conflict that made bond-rating agencies necessary. The moat is the corpus of reports, which only buyers collectively hold.
first_30_days: Build the fingerprint tool on 200 public reports from trust centres. Publish an 'Auditor Firm Quality Index v0' from public peer-review data. Offer security leads free re-verification of their vendor stack in exchange for contributing reports to the corpus, starting with those exposed to Delve's customer list.
